title: A Streetcar Named Desire
author: Tennessee Williams

sections.heading: Scenes 1, 2, 9, 10, and 11 (Key Dramatic Scenes)

epigraph.quote: Whoever you are—I have always depended on the kindness of strangers.

paragraphs:
SCENE ONE
The exterior of a two-story corner building on a street in New Orleans which is named Elysian Fields and runs between the L & N tracks and the river. The section is poor but, unlike corresponding sections in other American cities, it has a raffish charm. The sky that shows around the dim white building is a peculiarly tender blue, almost a turquoise, which invests the scene with a kind of lyricism and gracefully attenuates the atmosphere of decay. You can almost feel the warm breath of the brown river, and faint redolences of bananas and coffee. A tinny piano being played with the infatuated fluency of brown fingers is heard around the corner.

Stanley Kowalski and Mitch come around the corner. Stanley is about twenty-eight or thirty years old, roughly dressed in blue denim work clothes. He carries a red-stained package from a butcher's. He calls up to the first-floor window: 'Hey, Stella! Stella, baby!' Stella comes out on the first-floor landing: 'Don't holler at me like that. Hi, Mitch.' Stanley heaves the meat package up to her: 'Catch!' Stella cries out laughing: 'Stanley! What is it?' 'Meat!' he laughs, and heads for the bowling alley with Mitch.

Blanche DuBois appears around the corner of the building. She is daintily dressed in a white suit with a fluffy bodice, necklace and earrings of pearl, white gloves and hat, looking as if she were arriving at a summer tea or cocktail party in the country. Her delicate beauty must avoid a strong light. There is something about her uncertain manner, as well as her white clothes, that suggests a moth. She is carrying a valise and looking at a slip of paper.

Eunice looks down from the porch: 'What's the matter, honey? Are you lost?' Blanche speaks with faint shock: 'They told me to take a street-car named Desire, and then transfer to one called Cemeteries and ride six blocks and get off at—Elysian Fields!' Eunice nods: 'That's where you are, honey.' Blanche stares in disbelief: 'At Elysian Fields? These are—these are apartments?'

When Stella returns and embraces her sister, Blanche's nervous chatter reveals the desperate crisis that has driven her from Laurel, Mississippi: 'Stella, oh, Stella, Stella! Stella for Star! You haven't said a word to me! Look at me, don't look at that room, look at me! I won't stay here, Stella. It's not a suitable place for you to live!' But worse is yet to come. With trembling hands, Blanche breaks down: 'I lost Belle Reve, Stella! The ancestral home is gone! A woman alone in the world has got to be attractive, and I—I'm fading!'

The clash between Blanche's decaying Southern aristocratic fantasies and Stanley Kowalski's brutal, proletarian reality forms the tragic collision of the play. Stanley sneers at her furs, fake tiaras, and trunk of love letters. 'There's a Napoleonic code in Louisiana,' Stanley growls, slamming her trunk shut. 'Under which whatever belongs to the wife belongs to the husband and vice versa.' As the humid summer progresses, Stanley ruthlessly strips away Blanche's illusions, uncovering her scandalous past in Laurel, driving Mitch away, and culminating in the brutal violation that shatters her sanity forever.

In the final scene, as the doctor and nurse arrive from the asylum to lead her away, Blanche turns to the doctor, taking his arm with heartbreaking dignity: 'Whoever you are—I have always depended on the kindness of strangers.'
